extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a patent application specification adequately describes claimed subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (the written description requirement), including examiner procedures, evaluation criteria for species/genus claims, and handling of amended/new claims and priority claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors showing possession of claimed species
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession is a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors. Factors to be considered include the level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to conclude the applicant was in possession of the claimed species is sufficient. (See Eli Lilly, 119 F.3d at 1568.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Description requirement varies with nature and scope of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention at issue, and with the scientific and technologic knowledge already in existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents and printed publications in the art should be relied upon to determine whether an art is mature and what the level of knowledge and skill is in the art. In mature technologies where skill is high, written description questions generally should not be raised for claims present when originally filed (even if the specification discloses only a method of making and the function). (See Capon v. Eshhar; In re Hayes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater disclosure required in unpredictable or emerging technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions in emerging and unpredictable technologies, or for inventions characterized by factors not reasonably predictable, more evidence is required to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and the function may not be sufficient to support a product claim other than a product-by-process claim. Where process has actually been used to produce the product, written description for a product-by-process claim is satisfied; otherwise it may fail if it is not clear the acts can be performed or the product is produced. Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization may be insufficient. (See Fiers v. Revel; Amgen; Burroughs Wellcome.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests for species claims (must meet at least one)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any claim to a species that does not meet the test described under at least one of (a), (b), or (c) must be rejected as lacking adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The referenced tests (a)-(c) include (A) proof by actual reduction to practice, (B) reduction to drawings, or (C) disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure, properties, functional characteristics coupled with correlation) sufficient to show possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description support for genus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species by actual reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or by disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with correlation) or a combination thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure must be sufficient to show the applicant was in possession of the claimed genus. (See Eli Lilly, 119 F.3d at 1568.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative number of species requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'representative number of species' means that the species which are adequately described are representative of the entire genus; when there is substantial variation within the genus, one must describe a sufficient variety of species to reflect that variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of only one species supports a genus claim only if the disclosure 'indicates that the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the gen[us].' Courts caution that a patentee cannot necessarily claim a genus after describing only a limited number of species when unpredictability exists. (See Enzo Biochem; Noelle v. Lederman; In re Curtis; Rasmussen; In re Herschler; In re Smythe.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of species required is inverse function of skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes a 'representative number' is an inverse function of the skill and knowledge in the art; satisfactory disclosure depends on whether one of skill would recognize that applicant possessed the necessary common attributes of the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In unpredictable arts, a genus embracing widely variant species cannot be achieved by disclosing only one species. In predictable arts, less disclosure may suffice (e.g., disclosing an amino acid sequence may convey possession of the full genus of encoding nucleic acids because the genetic code is widely known).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification cannot support broad claims by describing only one embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification cannot always support expansive claim language merely by clearly describing one embodiment of the thing claimed; the issue is whether a person skilled in the art would understand applicant to have invented, and been in possession of, the invention as broadly claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification teaches only one particular method and there is no evidence that a more generic method was contemplated, broad claims can be invalid under 35 U.S.C. 112. (See LizardTech v. Earth Resource Mapping; Tronzo v. Biomet.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's initial burden when challenging written description
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasoning to explain why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the original disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must have a reasonable basis to challenge adequacy and must present by a preponderance of evidence why a skilled person would not recognize description in the applicant's disclosure. (See Wertheim.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Required express findings when rejecting for lack of written description
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact that support the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These findings should: (A) identify the claim limitation at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the filing date would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is insufficient. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments supported by the specification (mindful of prohibition against new matter). (See Rasmussen.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of applicant reply
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon reply by applicant, the examiner must again determine patentability of the claimed invention including whether written description is satisfied by reperforming the analysis in view of the whole record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the whole record demonstrates adequacy, do not repeat the rejection. If inadequacy remains, repeat the rejection, fully respond to applicant's rebuttal, and properly treat any further showings. Affidavits relevant to the written description must be thoroughly analyzed and discussed. (See In re Alton.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Each claim limitation must be supported in the original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with 35 U.S.C. 112 or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, or 365(c), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an explicit limitation in a claim is not present in the written description whose benefit is sought, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at the filing date that the description requires that limitation. Inherency requires that missing descriptive matter be necessarily present and recognized by persons of ordinary skill; probabilities or possibilities are insufficient. (See Hyatt v. Boone; In re Robertson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must include all elements applicant described as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must include all elements which applicant has described as essential; omission of an element described as essential may render a new or amended claim deficient under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the originally filed disclosure does not provide support for each claim limitation, or if an element applicant described as essential is not claimed, the claim must be rejected or the claim for priority denied. (See Johnson Worldwide; Gentry Gallery; Tronzo v. Biomet.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of adequacy and examiner's reasonable basis requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A description as filed is presumed to be adequate unless sufficient evidence or reasoning to the contrary is presented by the examiner to rebut the presumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently the examiner must have a reasonable basis and present a preponderance of evidence/reasoning to challenge adequacy. Rejection of an original claim for lack of written description should be rare. (See In re Marzocchi; In re Wertheim.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective standard for determining compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential question is whether the description clearly allows persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed; the disclosure must convey with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, the applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests and formulations include the 'does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill...to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed' (In re Gosteli) and 'convey with reasonable clarity...that the inventor was in possession' (Vas-Cath). The test for sufficiency in a parent application is whether the disclosure 'reasonably conveys to the artisan that the inventor had possession at that time of the later claimed subject matter.' (See Ralston Purina; In re Kaslow.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown in a variety of ways including description of an actual reduction to practice, by showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pfaff v. Wells Elecs.; Regents of the Univ. of California v. Eli Lilly; Amgen v. Chugai. Descriptive means include words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention. (See Lockwood.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonliteral description and amended claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of the claim need not be described literally in the specification to satisfy the written description requirement; however, if a claim is amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed, the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described in that application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conclusion leads to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (description requirement), or denial of the benefit of the filing date of a previously filed application, as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical circumstances where written description issues arise
rubrics_metrics.description: Description requirement issues typically arise in several circumstances where it must be determined whether claim subject matter is supported in the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common contexts include: (I) amendments affecting a claim; (II) reliance on filing date of a parent application under 35 U.S.C. 120; (III) reliance on priority under 35 U.S.C. 119; and (IV) support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference. (See MPEP §2163 for details and cited cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination procedure: complete patentability determination and communicate findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must complete the patentability determination under all relevant statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, 103) and clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and their bases in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After concluding analysis under all statutes, review proposed rejections and their bases to confirm correctness. The Office action should clearly communicate reasons and, when possible, offer helpful suggestions on how to overcome rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on the examiner: case-by-case factual inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry into whether the description requirement is met must be determined on a case-by-case basis and is a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner's analysis must set forth factual findings and reasoning supporting a conclusion of lack of written description. (See In re Wertheim.)
